https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/latvian-s.text: Chris Riches Updated Thu, 6 August 2026 at 12:23 pm UTC 0 Keaton Slater was killed on Radford Road in Coventry on Friday, June 14 (Image: Coventry Live/BPM MEDIA) A Latvian has been charged over the alleged hit-and-run death of a 12 year-old boy two years ago - after he was finally extradited to the UK. Schoolboy Keaton Slater died after being hit by a black BMW in Coventry on 14 June 2024 while on his way home from lessons just before the start of summer holidays. Efforts to extradite suspect Dolars Aleksanders, 23, from his native Latvia began after West Midlands Police named him as a person of interest shortly after the crash. On Wednesday night police said he was finally taken into custody at Gatwick Airport and appeared today at Birmingham Magistrates Court . He spoke only to confirm his identity and date of birth during the three-minute hearing and was remanded to appear at Birmingham Crown Court on September 3. District Judge David Wain told Aleksanders: "You have been returned to the United Kingdom in relation to these matters to face justice." Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said: "We have decided to charge Dolars Aleksanders with one count of causing death by dangerous driving following a police investigation into a fatal road traffic collision that led to the death of Keaton Slater. "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court to pursue criminal proceedings. "CPS West Midlands has worked closely with West Midlands Police, Home Office, the Latvian authorities, Europol, the Joint International Crime Centre (JICC), CPS International, and our Extradition Unit to bring Mr Aleksanders back to face proceedings in a UK court for an alleged crime that took place here." Efforts to extradite Aleksanders had been under way since police named him as a person of interest shortly after the crash. Parents Clint and Louise Slater said before the extradition that Keaton was "just walking home that day, doing nothing wrong." In tribute his older brother Josh added: "Two years on and still does not feel real. You touched the hearts of thousands and thousands of people, Keats. We will always keep your memory alive. "I wish you had the chance to grow up and had the chance to live your life. It just breaks my heart." Aleksanders was flown into Gatwick Airport on Wednesday and was then transported to a custody block in the West Midlands, police said. Dolars Aleksanders (Image: BPM MEDIA) West Midlands Police said on Wednesday evening: "A man has tonight (5 August) been charged over the death of 12-year-old Keaton Slater in Coventry after he was extradited from Latvia. "Dolars Aleksanders was detained last month and we've since worked with other agencies, including the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and National Crime Agency (NCA), to bring him back to the UK. "The 23-year-old was flown into Gatwick Airport earlier today and was then transported to a custody block in the West Midlands. "Aleksanders has now been charged with causing death by dangerous driving following the fatal hit-and-run collision in Radford Road in June 2024. "He has been remanded to appear before Birmingham Magistrates Court tomorrow (6 August). "Keaton's parents continue to be supported by specially trained officers. They have been fully updated around these developments and we thank them for their patience and support during our investigation." https://www.dw.com/en/how-climate-change.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mhsg A drone view of flood damage along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot district, Nepal. Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing . The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26. "This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone." With no time to prepare, families in Devighat returned to mud-filled homes days later to salvage whatever survived Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance How the disaster unfolded The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years. The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow. Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours. Relatives are going through photographs of missing people, trying to find loved ones Image: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance How did this happen? It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events. Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades. Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it. Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable. In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean. An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater. Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure. A disaster beyond adaptation Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one. Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation. The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in. "When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said. "Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come." https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-new.text: Internet Slovenia's .si domains boom after Trump calls AI 'superintelligence' Thursday, 01 Oct 2026 | 9:00 AM MYT share bookmark Related Stories Vietnam 22h ago Hanoi becomes world's fifth-fastest city for mobile Internet Climate 1d ago Robusta coffee’s climate resilience an ‘Internet myth’, new study says Technology 08 Oct 2026 India denies bias in satellite internet approvals after Musk's 'oligarchs' jab US President Donald Trump say he wants the term 'superintelligence,' abbreviated as SI, to be used worldwide instead of AI. — FABIAN SOMMER/dpa BUDAPEST : US President Donald Trump's preference for the term "superintelligence" over artificial intelligence has triggered a surge in registrations for Slovenian Internet domains, whose ".si" suffix matches his preferred abbreviation. Trump told the UN General Assembly in New York last week that he considered the term artificial intelligence, or AI, inappropriate because it made the technology "sound fake." Instead, he said he wanted the term "superintelligence," abbreviated as SI, to be used worldwide. Since then, the number of domains registered in Slovenia has surged to more than 200,000, compared with around 3,500 in the previous month, according to register.si, the authority responsible for administering Slovenian domain names. The agency said the sharp increase began following Trump's remarks. "Despite the greatly increased number of requests to all Registry systems, all services are operating smoothly," register.si said, adding that it would closely monitor operations and take measures if necessary. The authority rejected media speculation that it stood to make millions from the increased interest in ".si." It also advised owners of brands, slogans and companies that do not yet have a ".si" domain to register one as soon as possible. Trump has increasingly weighed in on the debate over the risks of artificial intelligence, after it emerged that recent models were showing deceptive behaviour and attempting to hack websites. Trump argued after meeting AI executives in Washington that AI companies should largely supervise each other, arguing that it was important for the US to keep a lead over China. UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned against "technology without accountability,” calling for safety standards and independent oversight mechanisms and saying "killer robots” should have no place in the future. – dpa Related stories: Trump launches America.gov in AI push for federal services Trump renames AI 'super intelligence' as leaders jostle over dangers Follow us on our official WhatsApp channel for breaking news alerts and key updates! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr86.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ambulances lined up outside Wainwright Health Centre after the deadly blast at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright By Kelly Ng Published 18 October 2026, 04:23 BST Updated 1 hour ago Several people have been killed or injured as a result of a large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta, the nation's defence minister has said. David McGuinty did not confirm the cause or the number of casualties, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate". The Canadian military and local authorities were managing the fire, he said. Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases. Canadian TV network Global News reported that at least seven were killed and dozens more injured when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding that his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected". The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) said Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton had declared a code orange, a disaster response protocol for responding to a high-casualty incident. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor there, told the broadcaster that the number of patients would otherwise "overwhelm" Edmonton's healthcare facilities. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster." After the fire erupted on Saturday, it "spread rapidly due to high winds" and tore through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said. The region experienced gusts of up to 100km/h (62mph), though local officials indicated fire crews had contained the blaze. The defence minister told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory". It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT). Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way. The mayor of the nearby town of Wainwright, Bruce Pugh, said it was a "heavy day" for his community. "We have neighbours who are either serving or former members of the Canadian Armed Forces. We're integrated, our kids play in the same hockey teams, attend the same schools," he told CBC. While details on the impact of the fire remain unclear, Pugh said he believed this would come to be the area's largest-ever mass casualty event. Image source, Google Image caption, Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is a busy military training base used for live-fire exercises Alberta's Premier Danielle Smith said the "significant and tragic fire" was "affecting many of [the province's] brave military personnel". Neighbouring provinces have mobilised in support. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said he had deployed resources to Alberta and was "ready to provide more if required", while British Columbia Premier David Eby said his government had offered "all possible assistance". Wainwright is the main base used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, according to CBC, with about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers on-site on a typical day. https://www.anothermag.com/art-photograp.text: October 30, 2026 Text Dominique Sisley Lead Image Photography Harley Weir. Courtesy of the artists and IDEA On a Monday morning in late October, I received two missed calls from Harley Weir . I’d not spoken to the photographer since I last interviewed her over a year ago. Strangely, just minutes before, my editor asked me to speak to her again, this time about Witch , a new zine made in collaboration with fashion designer Dilara Fındıkoğlu , exploring ancient magic and the innate power of women. When I called Weir back, she was apologetic, admitting that she’d accidentally dialled me from her pocket (“it was a butt dial!”). A coincidence – though given the subject, an eerily well-timed one. Witch feels a natural extension of Weir’s long-standing preoccupations. Her photographs have always been imbued with an earthy, almost primordial mysticism, documenting the feminine body in its various states of transformation. Her vision of womanhood is complex: tender, sexual, at times even grotesque. “People have historically been afraid of the natural woman,” Weir explains over Zoom when we catch up properly a few days later. “Her affinity with nature, her intuition, the ability to create life, which is a magical, crazy, unexplained thing that can’t really be controlled or understood.” In the background, the photographer’s newborn daughter gurgles. 11 Witch by Harley Weir and Dilara Findikoglu We’re soon joined on the call by Fındıkoğlu. Friends as well as collaborators, the pair share a fascination with feminine power, and the fears that have long surrounded it. In Witch , this interest comes into sharp focus. Shot over five days across Romania, the zine takes us inside dimly lit rooms crammed with candles, tarot cards and religious icons. In its portraits, Fındıkoğlu’s intricate corsetry – equal parts armour and adornment – lends the women a ceremonial, otherworldly presence. “The idea came about in conversation with creative director Matthew Scorțe, who is Romanian and told me tales of witches from his hometown,” says Weir, “and who better to team up with than Dilara, queen of the witches?” Fındıkoğlu, lighting up a Vogue and flicking her long, jet-black hair out of her face, elaborates: “We were trying to redefine the word ‘witch.’ Everyone is afraid of it because it’s associated with something evil, something dangerous. But we wanted to show that these powers are completely natural and that we all carry them within us.” Alongside the images, Witch features conversations with seven women from Romania, conducted by Weir and Fındıkoğlu. Among them are a practising Roma witch, a trans activist and sex worker, a journalist, and a body-modification artist. Each has her own relationship with the figure of the witch – for some, it represents a serious spiritual tradition; for others, a symbol of independence. “Many witches in Romania are highly paid; they’re doing well,” says Weir. “They’re still thriving. It’s not like it’s this hidden thing over there.” For Fındıkoğlu, the idea of the witch speaks to something more universal. “I think we’ve become so obsessed with understanding and rationalising everything that we’ve lost touch with the mystery of being human,” she says. “I feel like we’re already otherworldly beings in so many ways. There’s so much magic within us that we don’t even recognise. Why is the word magic understood as something we can‘t achieve?” Below, in an extract from the zine, four of the women featured in Witch reflect on their own experiences. Photography Harley Weir. Courtesy of the artists and IDEA Mihaela Minca Mihaela Minca is a practising Roma witch who describes herself as belonging to the “most ancient lineage” of witches on Romanian soil “We, Roma people – who are born and raised in Romania – are living history. Our legacy is passed down through trauma and blood. Witchcraft is both an innate birthright and a sacred gift. However, all women possess this magical power within themselves. The importance is to express, embody and use it. When she does, she becomes a very powerful woman. Magic lives in the heart of every woman on this earth. “In the Roma community, women are traditionally expected to live in closed circles, suppressing their opinions and living without a voice. Fortunately, the witch lineage that I’m a part of gave me a platform to express myself .” Antonella Antonella is a Romanian Roma trans woman, sex worker, tarot reader and activist who has campaigned for trans visibility and rights in her home country “I’ve been working in the sex industry for the past 20 years. I’ve experienced a lot of street violence, harassment, violation and discrimination. I always try to see the good in everything [...] Sunshine will find its way onto your path. “Seeing nobody talking about trans women [in Romania], I stepped forward as a political candidate. [Because of] heavy backlash from churches and conservative movements asking how a ‘hooker’ could run, I didn’t win, but it was something new for Romania and provided a platform for the trans community. I also wrote about my life because I wanted to leave something behind, and this started my trans activism in Romania. It stirred a lot of protest, but ultimately a lot of movement. “My past will never heal. Maybe I don’t want my wounds to heal. These wounds, both emotional and physical, have made me the powerful woman that I am today.” Photography Harley Weir. Courtesy of the artists and IDEA Andra Muresan Andra Mureșan is a Romanian journalist whose work investigates violence against women, sexual abuse and the growing threat of image-based abuse “I report on deepfake abuse and sexual violence in Romania […] I see women constantly being blamed, even though society is the one at fault. Over the last year, I struggled to stay focused on my purpose as a journalist. My last article documented two sexually abused women who were ignored and blamed by the police, judges and prosecutors. I realised then that my writing is my weapon. “When I was little, I used to see a witch as a fictional character. Then, as I got older, I understood the history of it more [...] the witch trials, and how this affected our rights as women […] Our rights are never guaranteed to stay the way they are today. If our rights are dismantled, we’ll have to come together [and use] our power as ‘witches’.” Maria Maria is a Romanian body-modification artist and science student whose experiments with piercing explore the limits of the body and conventional ideas of feminine beauty “I’ve had every weird haircut and possible piercing [...] I’ve had people yell at me on the street or even hiss like vampires. I guess, as women, we’re used to it and just brush it off. [...] I always liked a more alternative style, and what I did to my body felt beautiful to me. I do think it makes men uncomfortable because they feel like they’re losing power. We’re born into rules we never chose, and while breaking them threatens their power, other women also judge us for stepping out of line. “Doing whatever you want is liberating, but so is facing negative reactions without letting them break you. It’s freeing to realise you’ve moved past the anxiety of keeping yourself boxed in. Breaking free gives me an adrenaline rush and makes me happy. It’s sad seeing people stay stuck instead of doing the work to free themselves.” Harley Weir and Dilara Fındıkoğlu ’s Witch is released on 31 October, published by IDEA Art & Photography In Their Words Dilara Findikoglu Harley Weir Witchcraft Photography IDEA Books Subscribe to the weekly AnOther newsletter Thank you, you are now subscribed to AnOther The best of anothermag.com, published every Friday.
